fantasypoints.summary:
- **De’Von Achane** — Malik Willis’ low RB-target history is too noisy to fade Achane; he should still dominate designed passing-game work, even if Bobby Slowik adds some volatility. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Jaylen Warren** — Aaron Rodgers’ RB-targeting tendency keeps Warren’s receiving floor very strong, and his routes were already among the most efficient in fantasy. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **JK Dobbins** — Bo Nix’s heavy RB-target volume helps the Denver backfield, and Dobbins looks like the slightly better ADP bet than RJ Harvey thanks to health, the extension, the line, and stronger rushing efficiency. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Kenneth Gainwell** — Rodgers’ penchant for targeting RBs makes Gainwell’s receiving efficiency especially valuable in PPR formats. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Dylan Sampson** — Shedeur Sanders would be the better setup for Browns RB receiving volume, and Sampson’s receiving profile gives him the best best-ball upside relative to ADP. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Rico Dowdle** — Rodgers’ age-driven RB targeting gives Dowdle a meaningful receiving floor in this backfield. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Quinshon Judkins** — The Monken-style split backfield points him more toward the rushing side, leaving less receiving upside than Sampson. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **RJ Harvey** — Denver’s messy RB rotation makes Harvey the less attractive ADP play versus Dobbins. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Aaron Rodgers** — His 22.1% RB-target rate is a clear boost for pass-catching backs in his offense. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Bo Nix** — He funnels a lot of throws to RBs, giving Denver backs real receiving-volume support despite the rotation. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Shedeur Sanders** — His higher RB-target rate would meaningfully lift Browns backfield receiving usage compared with Deshaun Watson. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Deshaun Watson** — His lower RB-target rate suppresses the Browns’ receiving upside out of the backfield relative to Sanders. Jake Tribbey [1]
- **Malik Willis** — His historical RB-target rate is so noisy that it shouldn’t be used to downgrade Achane’s receiving role. Jake Tribbey [1]

That keeps Cook firmly at the top of the fantasy chart and could create a small PPR bump for the secondary backs if the usage shifts. [4]

- **Jude Bowry (OT/OG)** — The Bills are giving Bowry a run at tackle to start his career, and the piece notes he could eventually pass Chase Lundt on the depth chart for the backup swing-tackle job. That’s an offensive-line development rather than a fantasy one, but it matters for Josh Allen’s protection and the team’s tackle depth. [2]

JAX.summary:
- **Bhayshul Tuten (RB)** — Entering camp as the Jaguars’ projected starter, with the note that he had the full offseason as the No. 1 back while Chris Rodriguez Jr. was injured. LeQuint Allen is also positioned for more touches than as a rookie, so this backfield is one of the biggest usage battles to watch for fantasy. [1]

- **C.J. Williams (WR)** — The sixth-round rookie has momentum after several standout offseason moments and is now competing for limited reps in a deep receiver room, with Josh Cameron also trying to earn an offensive role. That points to a real training-camp battle for whatever WR depth/rotation snaps are available behind the established top options. [1, 7]

- **Quintin Morris (TE)** — Morris and Hunter Long are battling for a roster spot behind Brenton Strange and the rookie tight ends, Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol. If Morris wins the job, it would mostly matter as depth, but the competition signals that Long’s hold on the No. 2/No. 3 TE pecking order is not secure. [1]

- **Ventrell Miller (LB)** — Miller is in pole position to replace Devin Lloyd in the Week 1 starting lineup, with training camp set to determine whether he locks down that role. It’s not a core offensive fantasy note, but it is a meaningful snap-share change on defense and an IDP watch point. [1, 8]
